source_text: Quapropter quamuis sit malum corruptio et quamuis non sit a conditore naturarum, sed ex eo sit, quod de nihilo factae sunt, tamen etiam ipsa illo regente et gubernante omnia, quae fecit, sic ordinata est, ut non noceat nisi naturis infimis ad subplicium damnatorum et exercitationem admonitionemque redeuntium, ut inhaereant deo incorruptibili maneantque incorrupti, quod unum est bonum nostrum, sicut per prophetam dicitur: mihi autem inhaerere deo bonum est. neque illud dixeris: non faceret deus naturas corruptibiles. in quantum enim naturae sunt, deus fecit; in quantum autem corruptibiles, non deus fecit; non est enim ab illo corruptio, qui solus est incorruptibilis. si haec capis, gratias age deo; si non capis, quiesce et noli temere nondum intellecta damnare subplexque illi, qui lumen est mentis, adtende, ut intellegas. cum enim dicitur "natura corruptibilis," non unum, sed duo nomina dicuntur. item cum dicitur "deus fecit" de nihilo, non unum, sed duo nomina audimus. redde ergo istis singulis illa singula, ut cum audis naturam, ad deum pertineat, cum audis corruptibilem, ad nihilum, ita tamen, ut ipsae corruptiones, quamuis non sint ex dei arte, in eius tamen potestate sint disponendae pro rerum ordine et meritis animarum. ideo recte dicimus ab illo esse praemium atque subplicium. ita enim non fecit corruptionem, ut possit corruptioni eum dare, qui corrumpi meruerit, id est qui se ipse coeperit peccando corrumpere, ut cruciantem sentiat corruptionem inuitus, qui blandientem commisit uolens.
thought_title: Corruption is ordered by God for punishment and return
orientation: Augustine is concluding his argument that corruption is not from God as a nature but is ordered by God's governance for punishment and for calling souls back to him.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore although corruption is an evil and although it is not from the creator of natures, but it is from this, that they were made from nothing, nevertheless even this corruption itself, while he rules and governs all things which he made, has been so ordered that it may harm only the lowest natures for the punishment of the damned and for the training and admonition of those returning, so that they may cling to the incorruptible God and remain incorrupt, which is our one good, as it is said through the prophet: but for me to cling to God is good. And do not say this: God would not make corruptible natures. For insofar as they are natures, God made them; but insofar as they are corruptible, God did not make them; for corruption is not from him who alone is incorruptible. If you grasp these things, give thanks to God; if you do not grasp them, be still and do not rashly condemn things not yet understood, and as a suppliant attend to him who is the light of the mind, so that you may understand. For when it is said 'corruptible nature,' not one thing but two names are said. Likewise when it is said 'God made from nothing,' we hear not one thing but two names. Therefore give back to these single names those single things, so that when you hear nature, it may pertain to God, when you hear corruptible, it may pertain to nothing, yet in such a way that the corruptions themselves, although they are not from God's art, are nevertheless in his power to be arranged according to the order of things and the merits of souls. Therefore we rightly say that reward and punishment are from him. For he did not make corruption in such a way that he could give to corruption him who deserved to be corrupted, that is, him who began to corrupt himself by sinning, so that he may feel the torturing corruption unwillingly, who committed the flattering corruption willingly.

choices.why: The glossary and context use 'punishment' for the penalty of the damned; the spelling is a variant of supplicium.
The verb inhaerere means to adhere or cling closely; 'cling' preserves the physical intimacy of the Latin and matches the psalm quotation.
The phrase is a key distinction Augustine is analyzing; keeping the adjective-noun order as in Latin preserves the two-name analysis that follows.
Ars here means God's craftsmanship or skill in making; 'art' preserves the sense of divine making without importing 'design' or 'workmanship' which would be interpretive.
Blandientem means coaxing or flattering; Augustine contrasts the seductive corruption of sin with the torturing corruption of punishment, so 'flattering' captures the seductive sense.

bible_refs.note: mihi autem inhaerere deo bonum est

pass_b_english: Therefore, although corruption is an evil and although it does not come from the creator of natures but from the fact that they were made from nothing, nevertheless even corruption itself, under the rule and governance of the one who made all things, is so ordered that it harms only the lowest natures, for the punishment of the damned and for the training and warning of those who are returning, so that they may cling to the incorruptible God and remain incorrupt. For this alone is our good, as it is said through the prophet: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28 (LXX/Vulgate numbering)). And do not say, “God would not make corruptible natures.” Insofar as they are natures, God made them; but insofar as they are corruptible, God did not make them. For corruption is not from him who alone is incorruptible. If you grasp this, give thanks to God; if you do not grasp it, be still and do not rashly condemn what you have not yet understood, but humbly attend to him who is the light of the mind, so that you may understand. For when we say “corruptible nature,” not one but two names are spoken. Likewise when we say “God made from nothing,” we hear not one but two names. So give back to each of these its own: when you hear “nature,” let it belong to God; when you hear “corruptible,” let it belong to nothing—yet in such a way that the corruptions themselves, although they are not from God’s art, are still in his power, to be arranged according to the order of things and the merits of souls. Therefore we rightly say that reward and punishment come from him. For his not making corruption still leaves him able to hand over to corruption the one who deserved to be corrupted—that is, to the one who first began to corrupt himself by sinning, so that he who willingly committed it when it enticed should feel torturing corruption against his will.

problems.why: Latin says 'so that he could give him to corruption,' not 'could not give corruption.' The negative flips Augustine's meaning entirely.
problems.fix: so that he could give him to corruption

problems.why: 'Blandientem' modifies the person/sin, not corruption itself. It means 'the one who enticed/flattered,' referring to the sinner's own willing embrace of sin, not 'flattering corruption.'
problems.fix: who willingly committed it when it enticed

problems.why: Augustine's Latin follows the Septuagint/Vulgate numbering where this is Psalm 72:28, not Psalm 73:28. The Hebrew numbering differs by one for Psalms 9-147.
problems.ruling: Latin Vulgate Psalms 1-147 differ from Hebrew by one; Augustine's citation is Ps 72:28, not 73:28.

problems.quote: For he did not make corruption in such a way that he could give to corruption the one who deserved to be corrupted
problems.source_quote: ita enim non fecit corruptionem, ut possit corruptioni eum dare, qui corrumpi meruerit
problems.why: The English makes God's not making corruption block his handing the sinner over. The Latin says that not-making still leaves him able to do so.
problems.fix: For his not making corruption still leaves him able to hand over to corruption the one who deserved to be corrupted
problems.ruling: Latin 'ita non fecit corruptionem, ut possit... dare' says not making corruption leaves him able to hand over the sinner. The English reads as if the way he made it blocked that.

fixed: negation is real: preceding 'reward and punishment are from him' requires ability, so Latin 'ita non fecit corruptionem, ut possit corruptioni eum dare' means his not making leaves him able to hand over, not blocks it.
